rope
Someone is waiting on a jetty.

Dad was late and the tide was taking the boat away from the ladder. I had one foot on the jetty and one on the side of the boat, which was a ridiculous position to be in but I couldn't seem to stop. If I let go the rope would go underneath. He'd tied it wrong again. I shouted for the boy fishing further along to come and hold it. He couldn't hear, or didn't want to leave his rod. In the end I sat down hard on the wet planks and pulled the boat in with both hands. Dad came back with two bags of groceries. He said I thought you were staying aboard. I wanted to shout at him but he had bought the biscuits I like and was holding them out, not understanding what he'd done.
the spare coat
A useful thing is difficult to give away.

I gave the coat to the woman collecting for the shelter and then drove after her van. It was a stupid thing to do. She pulled over thinking something had fallen out. I couldn't explain it properly, just kept saying the blue one, the big blue one. There were several blue ones. We stood in a layby going through bags of other people's clothes until I found his. It didn't even smell of him any more. She was kind about it which made me cry worse.

I said I'd wash it and bring it to the depot. She said I didn't have to. But I do want someone to have it. I don't want it in the hall every day. I just wasn't ready for it to already be on somebody else.
low tide
A familiar route is blocked.

We used to walk the low-tide path to avoid paying for the ferry. They fenced it off this year. My aunt said fences were suggestions and lifted the bottom wire while I passed her bag underneath. Then she got stuck. Not properly stuck, her earring caught, but she began laughing and every time she laughed it pulled harder. The ferry man was watching from his hut. I could see his orange jacket. He'd watched us do this for thirty years and now he came out carrying wire cutters.

Technology fails at the worst possible moment.

FULL update not the little restart lie they tell you. i was mid sentence about being reliable and it just went blue. so i joined on my phone except i couldn't remember the password so now i'm on the phone to my own mother asking for the code because i used her email when i first made the account at uni. she keeps asking is this a scam rory. yes mum my whole professional life is a scam apparently. also the only decent shirt i own is still wet at the cuffs so im holding my arms out like a surgeon while she reads each number twice. she wants to know what the job is. i told her yesterday. she asks if theres a pension. work chat
Someone sends a message to the wrong group.

it was only a screenshot of the rota. fine technically it was a screenshot of the rota with a message underneath saying he couldnt organise a piss up in an actual functioning pub but the rota was the MAIN content. now he's seen it and put a thumbs up. not angry not anything just that little yellow hand. i can live with being shouted at i cannot live with a thumbs up. i tried deleting it and it deleted from my side only so for everyone else it's still there and for me there's an empty space where my career used to be. alex has sent me 'mate' privatly. just mate. cheers for the emergency response team alex glad you're on it
Untitled Sprint
A small inconvenience takes over someone's day.

been trying to return these headphones for forty minutes and the form asks what country they were manufactured in. why would I know that i bought headphones not a facotry. looked on the box it says designed in california which is where they want you to imagine them existing i guess. actually made in a warehouse of tiny wizards. put that in the box. now the form wont let me go back and i'm scared pressing submit will somehow make this legally binding
version two
Imagine sharing everyday life with a copy of yourself.

so version two of me would remeber to charge things. that is literally all i want from a clone. people always go oh but would it have a soul would it be you. don't care can it put the bike lights on charge. this version of me is tired. the clone can do monday to wednesday and i'll do thursday onwards. except then it'll want weekends which is fair but also defeats the point. maybe we alternate. now i'm inventing shared custody of my own life. it'd probably use all my good socks and tell people im the weird one. actually the more i think about this the more i think we need a third version to referee and that sounds expensive
the green room
A house is being emptied.

The men had taken the bed apart before asking what to do with the woman in it. She was not dead, which made the situation rather awkward. She sat up between the dismantled posts and asked for tea. Outside, her son was negotiating the price of the garden statues. He had been negotiating things since nine o'clock and hadn't come upstairs once. Mrs Vale put on her stockings slowly. One of the men handed her the other shoe. He was young and visibly frightened of her, although she had said nothing unkind. The mattress was already on the floor. It was the first time in sixty years that she could get out of bed without her feet hanging above the carpet.
Hem
Something borrowed does not fit.

The dress was too narrow across the back. If she breathed normally the seam would go, so she stood in the bathroom taking tiny breaths while the wedding started without her. She had borrowed it from a woman she disliked. That seemed significant at the time. There was a pair of nail scissors beside the basin and she considered opening the seam herself, just a little, in a place that wouldn't show.

Someone tried the door. Her sister. Then their mother. The organ began again, louder. She put one blade under the stitches. It was surprisingly hard to cut somebody else's dress. She kept thinking of the woman smoothing it over the hanger, saying it's vintage, you know, and the way she'd looked at her waist.
ribbon
You find an object inside a wall.

Inside the plaster was a ribbon, folded and folded until it was thicker than a matchbox. I pulled it free and it kept coming. Red, then brown with dust, then red again. My husband told me to stop because it might be tied to something important. What important part of a house is held up by ribbon? I said. But it had gone tight. Far above us, in the ceiling, a small weight dragged across the boards.
Afternoon
A guest arrives early.

She was early because she didn't want him to have time to hide anything. This sounded less mad before she arrived. Now she was on his doorstep at quarter past two holding an absurd bunch of lilies, watching him eat something straight from a pan. He wasn't dressed. Nobody was hiding in the curtains. There were no unfamiliar shoes. She said she'd written the time down wrong and he let her in, still chewing. The room smelled of frying onions. It was exactly the same room and she had used up all her anger preparing for a different one. She put the flowers in the sink. He asked what was wrong with her face, and then, more gently, whether she wanted some lunch.
the stairs
Someone has changed your house while you were away.

The staircase had been carpeted over while they were away. Their suitcases stood in the hall like witnesses. Neither of them had asked for a carpet. It was a dense floral thing, red roses on black, and it covered the first flight but stopped at the turning. Above that the steps were bare. She crouched to touch the edge. Fresh glue. Her husband was already on the phone to the letting agent saying unacceptable in his loud work voice. She wished he would be quiet. There were footprints in the pile, coming down. Whoever had put the carpet there was still somewhere above them. She tried to say his name without making a sound.
toll
A quest requires exact change.

We had six gold crowns, a ruby and the royal seal, but the toll was two copper pennies. The dwarf would not change a crown. There was a shop back in the village, he said. We'd come through that village three days ago. Pell offered him the ruby outright. Now he thought we were trying to bribe him, which apparently had a separate fine. I sat on the bag of provisions while they argued. On the far bank the dragon had started burning the watchtower. You could see the smoke. The dwarf looked over his shoulder and said the bridge might be closing early. I asked whether that meant we could cross for free before it shut and he started explaining the difference between a closure and a waiver.
provisions
Someone packs badly for an adventure.

We took eleven swords and no spoon. That sums it up really. I was only responsible for the maps but somehow everyone was angry with me about the spoon. Mira tried eating the stew with the flat of her dagger and cut her lip. We were one day into a journey supposed to last six months. I suggested carving spoons. Nobody had a suitable knife, despite all the swrods. By the time we got the fire going again the stew had become a black disc in the pot and a wolf had taken the bread. It didn't even run. It walked away while we were watching it because we'd all leaned our weapons against a tree on the other side of camp.
Wrong cave
A hero reaches the wrong destination.

There wasn't a dragon in the cave. There were bats, wet boots, and a very angry hermit who wanted to know why we'd kicked his door in. The map said HERE in red. I showed him. He turned the map over. More writing. 'Other cave,' it said. Pell said that hadn't been there before. He says that whenever we get lost. The hermit wanted four silver to repair the door and wouldn't accept a promise from the king. Sensible, to be fair.
the shutter
A shop opens for the last time.

By ten the shop was full of people who had never bought anything there. They took photos of the sign and said it was a shame. Mr Lau sold three batteries and a packet of mints. I was helping him put price stickers on the shelves because the shelves were for sale too. A woman asked whether she could have the old till as a decorative object. It was still plugged in. He said come back at five. She said she couldn't. He said then no. After she left we moved the till behind the counter where nobody would see it. His daughter arrived with sandwiches and began arguing with him in the back. He wanted to open tomorrow as well. I kept sticking labels on things, trying not to hear.
two seats
Someone saves a seat for a stranger.

The woman spread her coat across the seat and said somebody was coming. Nobody came. We went six stops. I was standing beside her with a box that was getting heavier by the minute, so I asked whether the person had missed the bus. She shook her head. Then she lifted the coat a little and showed me the bag underneath. It was moving. A cat, I thought, but it was a small chicken. She looked frightened. You're not meant to bring animals, she said. I told her the bus didn't have a chicken rule as far as I knew. She shifted the bag onto her knees and I sat down. Its head came out once near the hospital. Nobody said anything.
Change
A familiar person does not recognise you.

The man in the corner shop asked if I wanted a bag. He's asked me for fifteen years, although I always have one. Today I said yes. He reached under the counter and then looked up, properly looked. You moved away? he asked. I said no. He said your sister used to come. I don't have a sister. We both waited for the other to sort it out. The queue behind me grew. I paid for the milk and took the bag even though I didn't need it.
outside number eight
A delivery cannot be completed.

There were seventeen parcels for number eight and nobody at number eight. I checked the address twice. The driver was new and sweating through his shirt. Could I take them, he asked. I had come out to put the bins away, so now apparently I was in charge of the street. We carried boxes into my hall until I couldn't open my kitchen door. At lunchtime a woman knocked and said those were hers. She lived at eighteen. I'd already signed. The driver was in another town. We started carrying them down the road one at a time. By the third trip we were laughing. By the seventh she told me they were all exercise equipment and we stopped laughing.
rules
Friends disagree about a game.

'You can't move backwards.' 'You JUST moved backwards.' 'I'm a wizard.' 'You were a plumber ten minutes ago.' 'I multiclassed.'

We were supposed to be playing a board game I'd bought in a charity shop and none of us had noticed the instuctions were for a different game. So basically Tom had been making up rules for an hour and somehow still losing. I wanted my money back from Tom specifically. He said you can't demand a refund during a battle. I tipped the box over to find the real instructions and about thirty more pieces came out. Tiny sheep. We hadn't used a single sheep. Everyone went quiet because now we had to decide whether to start again or pretend sheep didn't exist.
the key
Two friends wait outside a locked door.

'You've got it.' 'No you've got it.' 'I gave it to you.' 'When.' 'When I gave it to you.' Excellent evidence from counsel there. We checked every pocket. I checked pockets in a coat I wasn't wearing. Then Luke said maybe it was still in the door. It was. On the other side. You could see the little shadow of it through the keyhole. 'Can we push it out?' I said. 'With what?' He held up my bank card. 'That is not going to fit.' 'We can fold it.'
Reset
A game changes while you are playing.

The character stopped obeying me halfway across the bridge. I pushed left and he sat down. Pressed jump, he took his shoes off. 'Controller's broken,' said Mat. We swapped. Same thing. On screen the little guy was wringing water out of his socks. There wasn't even water in this level. Mat tried shooting him with player two and missed because player two was lying down now. They were both exhausted. I said maybe we should give them a minute and Mat laughed, but he put the controller down. The game music kept going. The little guy looked directly at us. Then he started talking, no text box, just moving his mouth and pointing behind him at
cinema
Someone arrives with an extra ticket.

I had bought three tickets because I thought she was bringing her sister. She wasn't. Now she thought the third ticket was for my girlfriend. I don't have a girlfriend. I said that too fast. Made it worse. 'We could find someone,' I said, as if I were proposing to collect a stranger from the pavement. She started laughing. Finally. Then she actually did it. Asked a bloke by the machines if he wanted to see a film. He was waiting for his wife. His wife wanted to come too. Suddenly I was at the desk trying to get FIVE seats together for a screening that started four minutes ago and the man was telling me it was unallocated seating and I could just go in.
Wrong door
An apology is interrupted.

'Before you say anything, I'm sorry.' The woman blinked at me. 'For what?' 'The thing with the bike.' 'What bike?' Wrong flat. I could have left then. I could have just said sorry again and moved on, but she was smiling and I started explaining the entire story. Including how I'd bent the wheel and tried to straighten it with a frying pan. She stopped smiling. Her husband came to the door. 'That was YOU?' Apparently the flats shared a bike cupboard. I had apologised to the wrong person in exactly the right place. The actual owner appeared behind me carrying the frying pan. I'd left it there. Didn't have a plan for this part.
worms
A garden after rain.

worms all over the path. i tried putting them back on the soil but they kept coming out. maybe they know something i don't. the rain had stopped and the path was drying in little islands around them. one was so long i thought it was two stuck together. picked it up with a leaf and it contracted so hard i dropped it. sorry worm. my hands smelled of wet pennies after. there isn't really a story here i just spent twenty minutes doing this
nest
You find something unfinished.

the nest was in the wheelbarrow. under the folded sack, not in the hedge where i thought birds were meant to build. three pale eggs, warm looking although i didn't touch them. i needed the wheelbarrow for the gravel. stood there being annoyed with a bird, then with myself for being annoyed. borrowed next door's. now i go round the long way to the shed becuase the mother sits on the fence and makes this noise like i'm the worst thing that's ever happened. i put a bit of string across the handles so nobody else uses it. dad thought it was a spider web and put his hand through. spent the afternoon waiting to see if she'd come back
the apple
Something ordinary stays after everyone leaves.

one apple left right at the top. can't reach it with the ladder and it won't fall when i shake the branch. the leaves are mostly gone now. you can see the crow damage on it from the ground, one dark hole. i keep thinking something should eat it before it freezes. i could leave it alone. probably should. the tree does not need me to manage its last apple. but it's the first thing i check when i open the curtain and today the branch was bare and i felt annoyed that i'd missed whatever happened. checked the grass. nothing there either.
backup
A backup version of you is out of date.

My backup self was six weeks out of date. That meant he still liked my ex and hadn't learned the new parking rules. I tried to catch him up over breakfast but he kept asking why he'd been activated. Fair question, difficult answer. I wasn't dying or anything. I just had two job interviews at the same time. Technically this is prohibited by the licence agreement, which he knew because he was the version of me who still read licence agreements. We argued for forty minutes and missed both interviews. Then he asked if he could have my old laptop. I said OUR old laptop, since I was trying to establish a cooperative framewrok, but that made it sound like we were married. Neither of us wanted to wash up.
meeting room
A future invention meets an ordinary problem.

The teleportation system worked perfectly except it wouldn't move anything that was touching anything else. This was a safety measure to avoid taking bits of wall with you. So the test subject had to jump. But then his clothes were touching him. We put him in a loose gown, which didn't solve anything if you think about it for two seconds, which apparently none of us had. Meanwhile the client was asking why our rival could teleport whole shipping containers. I said they had different ethical standards. They probably had different progammers. Then the test subject asked whether air counted and the lead engineer left the room. That wasn't encouraging. I wrote 'air?' on the whiteboard so we could come back to it.
sleep credit

If you sell eight hours of sleep, who wakes up tired? This is the part nobody explains in the adverts. I sold mine on a Friday and felt fine Saturday. Sunday also fine. Thought I'd found a loophole. Monday morning my wife said I'd been standing in the kitchen asleep for half an hour making the same cup of tea. The bank had collected the sleep late. There was a processing delay. I called customer services and they asked me to stay awake while they checked the account which felt quite rude considering. Then they offered me a sleep loan to cover the shortfall. At this point I realised it was just a bank. All the futuristic stuff was decoration. I still took the loan because I had to drive.
attempt 4
A time-saving device takes too long.

A machine to make time. Not save it, actually make another minute. It takes two minutes to run. That's the problem. You can paralellise them I suppose, but then you've invented a really noisy way to stand in a warehouse. Maybe the extra minute arrives yesterday so you could stop yourself buying the machine. Then who built it. I'm going in circles. The man switches it off and goes to lunch. His sandwich has vanished. That's something at least.
cups
Someone helps you move.

My sister unpacked the kitchen according to a system she understood. Plates above the sink, glasses by the oven, mugs somewhere I couldn't find. Every time I asked where something was she said it was obvious. I had moved to be closer to her. That was the thing neither of us wanted to say while we argued about cupboards. After she left I moved everything back to where I'd first put it. Then I couldn't find it either. I rang her to ask about the mugs and she answered immediately, before the first ring had finished. She'd been waiting in her car downstairs, worried she'd been too much. I told her to come back up. We ate takeaway out of the cartons because all the plates still had newspaper stuck to them.
spare bed
A guest stays longer than expected.

He said two nights, so I made the bed with the good sheets. By the ninth night I wanted those sheets back. They were mine and I had no spare set, only the thin ones that twist around your legs. It sounds petty written down. He had lost his job and probably his flat, although he wouldn't say the second part. Every evening he offered to cook. Every evening I said don't worry about it and then got angry that I was cooking again.

Tonight I said yes. He looked surprised. I sat in the kitchen while he chopped onions with my blunt knife. He didn't ask where anything was. He'd learned the cupboards. I wasn't sure whether that made me feel better or worse.
two teaspoons
An object you do not need.

There are two teaspoons in my handbag and I don't remember putting them there. I found them at the dentist when I was looking for my card. The receptionist waited while I moved them out of the way. One is my mother's. I know because the handle has a dent from the disposal. The other might be from work. I have become a person who carries stolen cutlery without noticing. Mum would have found this funny. I wanted to tell her, which still happens at completely ordinary times. I put them back in the bag. The dentist called my name and asked how I'd been. I said fine, automatically, then said actually no and started crying with a paper bib on.
first evening
A new home has unfamiliar sounds.

The first night I slept on the floor because the bed bolts were in the other van. Every time I rolled over the plastic under the mattress crackled. Upstairs someone walked from one end of the flat to the other, stopped, walked back. I tried to work out their rooms from the footsteps. Kitchen at the front, bedroom at the back, maybe a child who wouldn't settle. At three I went out onto the landing in my socks. The upstairs door was open and a man was carrying a sleeping baby around a pile of unpacked boxes. He looked as startled as I felt. We'd both moved in that day. Neither of us knew which bin was ours. We whispered about that for a while.
Letterbox
You receive a letter for someone else.

The letter was for the woman who used to live here. I'd returned the others but this one had a photograph sticking out, so I looked. A boy on a bicycle. On the back someone had written that he'd finally learned. I put it on the hall table and forgot it until the woman knocked on Saturday to ask about post. I gave her the bills first. I don't know why. When I handed her the photograph she held it by the edges and sat on the bottom stair without asking. I went to make tea. I wanted to give her privacy but it was my flat and the kettle was in the same room. She kept saying look at him, as if I knew who he was.
